title: Two problems called storage
bodyMd:
For two decades, utilities evaluating storage for electricity grids asked a single question: what does a kilowatt-hour of capacity cost to install? By that measure lithium-ion batteries have been an unambiguous success, and their falling installed cost is routinely offered as evidence that the storage problem has been solved. Yet the metric quietly assumes that every stored kilowatt-hour is worth the same, and on a grid dominated by wind and solar generation that assumption fails. The value of storage depends on how often the stored energy is cycled and on the spread between the prices at which it is charged and discharged. A battery that can be filled and emptied once a day earns its keep through many small arbitrages; a reservoir that must hold charge from a windy October until a still February earns nothing for months and must recover its entire cost from a handful of scarce, expensive hours.

This distinction has produced two largely separate engineering agendas. The first seeks ever-cheaper power electronics and faster response, and lithium-ion chemistry serves it well. The second seeks the lowest possible cost per unit of energy stored, and is close to indifferent to whether the round trip wastes half of what goes in; here iron-air cells, pumped water and underground hydrogen caverns compete, and lithium-ion is simply the wrong tool. Analysts who report a single "levelised cost of storage" collapse the two agendas into one number and, in doing so, reliably overstate how far the second has progressed.

The regulatory difficulty is that tariffs reward the first agenda and not the second. Payments for frequency response and for firm capacity accrue to assets that can act within seconds and be counted on daily; nothing pays an asset for the option value of energy that may be called on only in the worst week of a decade. Until that option is priced, the seasonal problem will remain unsolved — not because the engineering is impossible, but because no one is paid to solve it.
accessibilityText: A three-paragraph prose passage about electricity grid storage. It argues that the standard installed-cost metric hides a difference between daily-cycling storage, which lithium-ion batteries serve well, and seasonal storage, which needs the lowest possible cost per unit of energy and tolerates poor round-trip efficiency. The final paragraph says existing tariffs pay for fast response and daily firm capacity but pay nothing for the option value of rarely used seasonal energy, so the seasonal problem persists for commercial rather than technical reasons.
